items.stem: In a 1983 speech, President Reagan called the Soviet Union an 'evil empire.' A historian wants to use this speech as evidence about Reagan's Cold War strategy. Which evaluation of the speech as evidence is most accurate?

stimulus.text: In a 1983 speech, President Reagan called the Soviet Union an 'evil empire.' (The phrase is historical; context summarized for this item.)

options: (A) The speech is unreliable as evidence because presidential rhetoric always masks true intentions, so historians should disregard such speeches entirely when studying policy.
(B) The speech proves Reagan abandoned every form of diplomatic engagement with the USSR from 1983 onward.
(C) The speech mainly reveals Reagan's intended audience and framing — rallying conservatives and pressuring Moscow — rather than a literal policy blueprint.
(D) The speech's moral language proves détente never really happened and that Nixon and Kissinger had always treated the USSR as an irredeemable moral enemy.
items.explanation: A speech is evidence of how a leader framed an issue for an audience, not a transcript of policy. Reagan's 'evil empire' line rallied conservatives at home and put psychological pressure on Moscow. Reading it as a literal end to diplomacy, or dismissing it as evidence of nothing, are both sourcing errors.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. That rhetoric serves political purposes doesn't make it useless as evidence — it reveals intended audience and framing. 'Always masks' and 'disregard entirely' are the overgeneralization.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Harsh language didn't end diplomacy: Reagan later met Gorbachev repeatedly and signed the INF Treaty. Rhetoric is not policy.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The speech is best read as framing aimed at audiences — domestic conservatives and the Soviet leadership — rather than a literal policy blueprint.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Détente was real — SALT I, expanded trade, summit diplomacy. A later speech doesn't erase the negotiated coexistence of the 1970s.

items.stem: The chart shows crude oil prices collapsing from about $35.50 per barrel in 1980 to the mid-$20s by the late 1980s. What effect did this price collapse have on the Soviet economy?

chart_spec.title: Crude Oil Prices, 1973–1990 (nominal dollars per barrel)
chart_spec.source_note: Approximate figures; the 1980s oil-price collapse that squeezed Soviet export revenues, an internal pressure on the USSR alongside the factors in u9.md §What the exam tests here ('internal Soviet decay').

options: (A) The Soviet Union imported all of its oil and had to pay more for it.
(B) The price collapse single-handedly caused the breakup of the Soviet Union in 1991.
(C) The USSR lived on oil-export earnings; the 1980s price crash cut state revenue just as the arms race demanded more spending.
(D) The collapse helped the USSR because cheaper oil lowered the cost of its growing military buildup in the costly 1980s arms race.
items.explanation: The Soviet command economy could not produce competitive manufactured exports, so it paid for imported grain and technology with oil and gas earnings. When prices fell by roughly a third in the mid-1980s, that revenue stream shrank exactly when matching Reagan's buildup required more military spending — an internal economic squeeze that deepened the system's crisis.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The USSR was a major oil exporter, not an importer; the problem was falling export earnings, not rising import costs. Reversing who buys and who sells is the core mistake here.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. No single event ended the Soviet Union; historians point to a combination of causes, including nationalist movements, political reform, economic stagnation, and the winding down of the Cold War itself. One price drop, however painful, cannot carry the whole explanation alone.
option_explanations.C: Correct. It connects the chart's price collapse to the Soviet fiscal bind: shrinking hard-currency income arriving just as matching the American military buildup required more spending.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. A seller of oil is hurt when prices fall: the revenue lost from exports dwarfs any savings on the oil the military itself burns. Cheaper oil helps the buyers, not the USSR.

items.fact_source: u9.md §What the exam tests here — 'internal Soviet decay' as a required cause of the Cold War's end

items.stem: The 2003 invasion of Iraq was justified by claims about weapons of mass destruction that proved false. What was the chief political consequence of that failure?
options: (A) It single-handedly decided every presidential election after 2004 in the Democrats' favor.
(B) It proved that presidential claims about national security are always deliberately fabricated, permanently destroying public trust in the presidency.
(C) It directly caused the 2008 financial crisis, since war spending was the sole trigger of the recession.
(D) It discredited the neoconservative vision of preventive war and deepened the country's division over the long, costly occupation.
items.explanation: The missing WMDs destroyed the war's stated rationale. What followed — years of insurgency, thousands of American dead, trillions spent — turned the public against the intervention and split the country. The review's verdict is direct: the occupation 'split the country and discredited the neoconservative vision' of preventive war.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The WMD failure hurt Republicans in 2006 and 2008, but one event doesn't decide every election — Republicans won the presidency in 2004, 2016, and 2024. Be wary of single-cause explanations for decades of elections.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Faulty intelligence and cherry-picked evidence are not proof that every national-security claim is a deliberate lie, and public trust in the presidency has risen and fallen since. One case doesn't establish a universal rule.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The 2008 crisis was rooted in the housing bubble and subprime mortgage collapse. War spending deepened federal deficits, but it was not the sole trigger — that something came first doesn't mean it caused what followed.
option_explanations.D: Correct. False premises plus a grinding, costly occupation discredited the doctrine behind the war and divided the nation over it.

items.fact_source: u9.md §The story — 'the invasion of Iraq on claims about weapons of mass destruction that proved false. Iraq's long, costly occupation split the country and discredited the neoconservative vision'

items.stem: Barack Obama's election in 2008 was historic as the first Black presidency, and some commentators called it a 'post-racial' milestone. What does the review's later account suggest about that reading?
options: (A) The reading was fully confirmed: racial conflict disappeared from American politics entirely after 2008, never to return.
(B) The reading was premature: racial conflict continued through Black Lives Matter and demographic-change politics.
(C) The reading was irrelevant because Obama's race was never mentioned during the campaign.
(D) The reading was proven by the immediate repeal of all civil rights laws.
items.explanation: The review presents Obama's election as genuinely historic but not transformative of racial politics: it then describes Black Lives Matter organizing, backlash politics around immigration and demographic change, and deepening polarization. Symbolism and structural conflict coexisted.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The review documents major racial-justice movements and conflicts after 2008, contradicting any claim that racial conflict ended.
option_explanations.B: Correct. It follows the review's narrative arc: a milestone election followed by, not replacing, ongoing struggles over race and identity.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Obama's race was widely discussed throughout the campaign and presidency; it was not ignored.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. No civil rights laws were repealed; the claim is factually false.

items.fact_source: u9.md §The story — Obama's 2008 election 'was read by some as a post-racial milestone'; later 'movements from Occupy to Black Lives Matter to #MeToo'

items.stem: A historian argues the chart shows immigration transformed America more after 1970 than in any earlier era. Which additional evidence would best test that claim?

chart_spec.title: Foreign-Born Share of U.S. Population, 1970–2020
chart_spec.source_note: Approximate census-based figures; the demographic change 'especially around immigration' described in u9.md §The story.

options: (A) The chart alone is sufficient; no further evidence is needed to prove the claim.
(B) Data on the foreign-born share around 1890–1910, when it reached similar levels.
(C) Recent polls of public opinion about current immigration levels.
(D) The total U.S. population count in 2020.
items.explanation: The historian's claim compares the post-1970 era with every earlier one, but the chart starts in 1970, so it cannot support that comparison by itself. The 1890 census recorded 14.8 percent foreign-born — a level that rivals the modern peak of 13.7 percent — so measuring the earlier peak is the evidence that would actually test whether the post-1970 transformation was the largest.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The claim is a comparison with earlier eras, and a chart that begins in 1970 supplies no earlier-era evidence at all. One source cannot prove a claim it does not cover.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The 1890 census recorded 14.8 percent foreign-born, a figure that rivals the chart's modern peak; evidence from the earlier high-water mark is what would show whether the post-1970 change was truly the largest.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. How Americans today feel about immigration says nothing about how large the demographic change was, past or present; opinions are not a measure of the foreign-born share.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The total population in 2020 cannot test a claim about immigration's transformative role; a single headcount gives no information about who was foreign-born, then or earlier.

items.fact_source: u9.md §The story — 'demographic change — the coming "majority-minority" nation — reshaped politics, especially around immigration' | 1890 census: 14.8% foreign-born (earlier peak rivaling the modern 13.7%)

items.explanation: The chart shows the national trend, and the review locates its costs: factories closed across the Northeast and Midwest — the Rust Belt — while growth shifted to the Sun Belt.
items.fact_source: u9.md §Added 2026-10-01 deindustrialization — factories closed across the Northeast and Midwest (the Rust Belt) while manufacturing's share of employment fell nationally from roughly a quarter of jobs around 1970 toward about a tenth by 2010 (approximate)

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The review says the Sun Belt gained people and plants; it was the region of growth, not concentrated loss.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The review stresses that the costs were concentrated, not evenly spread.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The review does not name the rural West or farming; it names the Northeast and Midwest.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The review places the factory closures in the Northeast and Midwest, the Rust Belt.

options: (A) In the Sun Belt, where defense industries attracted new plants and population kept growing.
(B) Across all regions equally, since the decline was spread evenly throughout the country.
(C) In the rural West, where farming replaced factory work as the region's economic base.
(D) In the Northeast and Midwest, where factories closed across the Rust Belt.

items.explanation: Keynesian policy tools rested on the idea that inflation and unemployment moved in opposite directions, so policymakers could accept a little more of one to get less of the other. Stagflation — both rising together — broke that trade-off, which is why the review says it destroyed the Keynesian playbook.
items.fact_source: u9.md §Added 2026-10-01 deindustrialization — stagflation, inflation and unemployment rising together, 'destroyed the Keynesian playbook'

option_explanations.A: Correct. With inflation and unemployment rising together, the trade-off that Keynesian tools relied on no longer worked.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The 1970s had high inflation, not zero inflation.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Stagflation hit in the 1970s, before Reagan's 1981 tax cuts, and the review does not blame the tax cuts for it.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The review says stagflation destroyed the Keynesian playbook — the opposite of vindicating it.

options: (A) Keynesian tools assumed inflation and unemployment traded off; stagflation had both rising together.
(B) Keynesian economics required zero inflation at all times, a condition the 1970s economy delivered.
(C) Stagflation was caused by Reagan's 1981 tax cuts, which took effect before Keynesianism was ever tried.
(D) Keynesian economists welcomed stagflation as clear proof that their economic theories worked well.
items.stem: The review says the stagflation of the 1970s “destroyed the Keynesian playbook.” Why did stagflation pose such a problem for Keynesian economics?

items.explanation: The review draws a direct line: the 1970s broke the postwar industrial bargain, and the resulting resentment powered Reagan's 1980 victory and later populist revolts.
items.fact_source: u9.md §Added 2026-10-01 deindustrialization — the 1970s 'broke the postwar industrial bargain'; deindustrialization 'fed the resentment that powered Reagan's 1980 victory and later populist revolts'

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The review says voters repudiated the party in power — Reagan's 1980 election was a rejection, not a reward.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The review traces the resentment behind Reagan's 1980 victory and later populist revolts to deindustrialization.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The review says stagflation destroyed the Keynesian playbook; it did not strengthen faith in it.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The breakdown is presented as a failure of government economic management, not a success.

options: (A) It convinced voters to reward the party in power for its handling of the crisis.
(B) It fed the resentment that powered Reagan's 1980 victory and later populist revolts.
(C) It strengthened public faith in the Keynesian playbook as the right economic framework.
(D) It persuaded Americans that government management of the economy had succeeded.
items.stem: How did the economic breakdown of the 1970s set up the politics that followed, according to the review?

items.explanation: The review's figures describe the bargain at its height: manufacturing at roughly a quarter of jobs around 1970 and union membership at roughly a third of workers in the 1950s. The 1970s broke that arrangement.
items.fact_source: u9.md §Added 2026-10-01 deindustrialization — the 1970s 'broke the postwar industrial bargain'; at its height manufacturing held roughly a quarter of jobs (around 1970) and unions covered roughly a third of workers (1950s) (approximate)

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The review describes an economy built on factories and unions, not one without them.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The review describes private-sector industrial employment and union coverage, not guaranteed government jobs.
option_explanations.C: Correct. These are the review's own figures for the industrial economy at its height.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The review's story is about manufacturing, not agriculture.

options: (A) An economy with no factories and no unions anywhere in the country at all.
(B) An economy where the federal government guaranteed every single worker a permanent job.
(C) An economy with a quarter of jobs in manufacturing and a third of workers in unions.
(D) An economy where agriculture employed most American workers by a wide margin.
items.stem: The review says the 1970s “broke the postwar industrial bargain.” Drawing only on the figures the review gives, what did that bargain look like at its height?
